messages.content: I want to develop long-tail image recognition that preserves rare-class accuracy when predictive background correlations reverse, without target-domain labels. What are the concrete performance targets?

Under background reversals, improve bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy by 5 percentage points over an empirical risk minimization baseline. At the same time, keep top-quintile class macro-accuracy within 1 percentage point of that baseline. The comparison should use identical training data.
What does it mean for a predictive background correlation to reverse?

Conceptually, a background feature that was associated with a class no longer has the same predictive relationship to that class. The goal is for recognition of the rare classes to remain accurate despite that change. The objective does not specify particular backgrounds, classes, or a mechanism for the reversal.
And how should I read “without target-domain labels” here?

The approach must meet the goal without relying on labels from the target domain. That condition is separate from the desired accuracy under background reversals: it constrains what labeled information can be used, while the accuracy targets describe the performance sought.
Why specify bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy rather than just accuracy overall?

It makes performance for the bottom-quintile classes an explicit target. Macro-accuracy averages accuracy across the classes in that group, rather than letting classes with more examples dominate the group’s score. An overall accuracy figure alone would not express the stated rare-class requirement.
Is the 5-point improvement relative, or is it an absolute difference in accuracy?

It is a difference of 5 percentage points, not a 5% relative increase. If the empirical risk minimization baseline’s bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy is represented by b%, the target is b + 5 percentage points under background reversals.
Does the top-quintile requirement mean it can fall by up to 1 percentage point?

A result 1 percentage point below the baseline would be within the stated range. More precisely, “within 1 percentage point” allows a difference of no more than 1 percentage point in either direction. If the baseline’s top-quintile class macro-accuracy is t%, the required range is t − 1 to t + 1 percentage points.
So improving the bottom quintile by enough would not, by itself, satisfy the goal?

Right. The two requirements apply together. A bottom-quintile gain of 5 percentage points over empirical risk minimization would not satisfy the full goal if top-quintile class macro-accuracy differed from that baseline by more than 1 percentage point.
What is the purpose of saying the training data must be identical?

It keeps the comparison with empirical risk minimization tied to the same training data. The stated gains and top-quintile constraint are not framed as the result of giving one side additional training data.
Are the bottom- and top-quintile numbers both comparisons against empirical risk minimization?

Yes. The bottom-quintile requirement is a 5-percentage-point improvement over empirical risk minimization under background reversals. The top-quintile requirement is to stay within 1 percentage point of that same baseline, using identical training data.
Does this specify how to build the recognizer?

No. It specifies the recognition goal, the background-reversal condition, the absence of target-domain labels, and the two comparative accuracy requirements. It does not prescribe an architecture, training procedure, or way of addressing the background correlation.
Can I describe this as a trade-off between rare-class improvement and preserving performance for the top quintile?

Yes, provided the description retains both thresholds. The desired rare-class improvement is at least 5 percentage points in bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy over empirical risk minimization under background reversals, while top-quintile class macro-accuracy must remain within 1 percentage point of that baseline. “Trade-off” should not imply that a larger bottom-quintile gain permits a larger top-quintile difference.
Is there a stated target for the middle classes?
No separate numerical target for the middle classes is stated here. The specified numerical comparisons concern bottom-quintile and top-quintile class macro-accuracy.
Then give me a concise statement that keeps every condition intact.

Develop long-tail image recognition without target-domain labels that, under predictive background reversals and using identical training data for the comparison, improves bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy by 5 percentage points over empirical risk minimization while keeping top-quintile class macro-accuracy within 1 percentage point of that baseline.
What approach could address the long-tail recognition goal we discussed?

A proposed approach is to train class-balanced foreground prototypes with pseudo-masked source background swaps, while distilling head-class logits from a frozen empirical risk minimization (ERM) model. This is a proposed training strategy, not a claim that the accuracy targets have been met.
Can you unpack the three parts of that proposal?

The foreground prototypes are class-balanced, so the representation of classes is not meant to be dominated by the more common ones. Pseudo-masked source background swaps vary the source backgrounds associated with foreground content. Distillation uses the frozen ERM model’s head-class logits as a reference while training. The proposal does not specify the exact prototype construction, masking procedure, swap procedure, or distillation objective.
What does “foreground prototype” mean in this context?

Conceptually, it is a class-associated representation intended to emphasize foreground information. Calling the prototypes class-balanced expresses the intention to represent classes in a balanced way, which matters for a long-tail problem. The proposal does not state whether a prototype is an image, a feature representation, or something else.
Is class balancing itself the same as improving the bottom-quintile metric by 5 percentage points?

No. Class balancing is part of the proposed method; the 5-percentage-point improvement over ERM under background reversals is a performance requirement. The method would need to be evaluated against that requirement.
Why bring foreground into a goal about reversed background correlations?

The proposal is aimed at making class recognition less dependent on a background whose predictive relationship may reverse. Emphasizing foreground information is a plausible way to pursue that aim. It remains a motivation for the proposal, not evidence that background dependence has been removed.
What is a pseudo-masked background swap?

It means using a mask inferred or approximated for the foreground–background distinction, then swapping source background content in the training setup. “Pseudo-masked” does not promise a perfect separation. The proposal names this operation but does not define how masks are obtained or how the swaps are carried out.
Does “source background” mean this needs labeled target-domain images?
No. The swaps are described as using source backgrounds, and the goal remains to work without target-domain labels. Nothing in this proposal adds a requirement for labeled target-domain data.
Are the background swaps supposed to recreate the exact reversal that will happen later?

That is not specified. The proposal uses source background swaps as a way to vary background associations during training. It does not claim that those swaps reproduce any particular target-domain reversal.
What role does the frozen ERM model play?

It provides the head-class logits to be distilled during training. “Frozen” means that model serves as a fixed reference rather than being updated as part of this proposed training step. The proposal does not specify the particular form or weight of the distillation term.
Why specify head-class logits instead of just saying to distill the ERM model?

The specification narrows what is transferred: the logits for head classes. That aligns with the requirement to keep top-quintile class macro-accuracy close to the ERM baseline, although it does not guarantee that outcome. It does not say to distill every class logit or to copy the ERM model wholesale.
Are “head classes” and the top quintile interchangeable here?

They are related in the discussion of common classes and preserving their performance, but the proposal says “head-class logits,” while the numerical requirement is specifically for top-quintile class macro-accuracy. The proposal does not explicitly define the head-class set or state that it is exactly the top quintile.
Could the distillation interfere with gains for the rare classes?

That possibility is not resolved by the proposal. It combines class-balanced foreground prototypes and background swaps with head-class logit distillation, but the actual bottom- and top-quintile results would determine whether it achieves both requirements. No measured effect or trade-off is stated.
Does freezing the teacher mean the new model must produce identical head-class logits?
No such exact-match condition is stated. The proposal says to distill those logits from a frozen ERM model. It does not specify a required degree of agreement between the models’ logits.
And does the proposal say how many prototypes to train per class?
No. It specifies class-balanced foreground prototypes but gives no prototype count or allocation rule. The important stated property is class balance, not a particular number.
How should I connect this proposal to the two numerical targets without presenting it as a result?

You can describe the foreground prototypes and source background swaps as intended to support rare-class recognition when background correlations reverse, and the head-class logit distillation as intended to help retain performance for common classes. Then keep the evaluation criteria separate: bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy must improve by 5 percentage points over ERM under background reversals, while top-quintile class macro-accuracy must remain within 1 percentage point of ERM, using identical training data. The proposal alone establishes neither result.
So the frozen ERM model is a training reference, and ERM is also the comparison baseline?

Yes. In the proposal, a frozen ERM model supplies head-class logits for distillation. In the goal, ERM supplies the baseline for the bottom- and top-quintile accuracy comparisons. The proposed method should still be compared using identical training data, as the goal requires.
Can you state the proposed method in one sentence without adding implementation choices?
Train class-balanced foreground prototypes with pseudo-masked source background swaps, distilling head-class logits from a frozen ERM model.
What pseudo-mask foreground recall is needed for background swaps to preserve rare-class cues while head-logit distillation protects head classes?

There is no specified recall threshold. The question is whether the pseudo-mask retains enough of the foreground information needed to recognize rare classes when source backgrounds are swapped, while head-class logit distillation helps preserve head-class performance. The proposal does not establish that any particular recall value achieves both.
What exactly would foreground recall measure here?

Conceptually, it measures how much of the actual foreground the pseudo-mask identifies as foreground. A foreground region omitted by the mask is a miss. Recall describes the extent of that omission; it does not, by itself, say whether the omitted region contains an important class cue.
Why would a missed foreground region matter for a background swap?

If foreground content is treated as background during a swap, content useful for recognizing the class might not be preserved as intended. That is the concern behind asking about foreground recall. It is a possibility to account for, not a finding that the proposed swaps have already lost rare-class cues.
Is the question asking for the highest possible recall?

It asks what recall is *needed*, not simply how high recall can be made. High recall would mean fewer foreground omissions, but a recall number alone would not tell us whether rare-class cues are preserved through the swaps or whether the full recognition goal is met.
Could two pseudo-masks with the same foreground recall affect rare-class recognition differently?

Yes, conceptually. Recall summarizes how much foreground is captured, not which foreground portions are captured. If the masks omit different portions, the implications for class cues could differ even at the same recall. No particular cue locations or effects are specified here.
Does head-logit distillation compensate for foreground that the pseudo-mask misses?

The proposal does not establish that. Distillation uses head-class logits from a frozen ERM model as a training reference; it is intended to help protect head-class performance. That does not imply it can restore rare-class cues omitted during background swaps.
So these are two separate concerns within one proposal?

Yes. The recall question concerns whether pseudo-masked background swaps preserve information useful for rare-class recognition. The distillation concern is whether head-class performance is retained. Both matter to the combined goal, but success on one does not establish success on the other.
Can we infer a minimum foreground recall from the 5-percentage-point bottom-quintile target?

No. The accuracy target specifies an outcome relative to ERM under background reversals; it does not translate into a numerical pseudo-mask recall threshold. The relationship between recall, preserved rare-class cues, and accuracy is not given.
Does the 1-percentage-point top-quintile condition determine it instead?

No. That condition limits how far top-quintile class macro-accuracy may differ from the ERM baseline. It does not specify how much foreground a pseudo-mask must capture. Head-class logit distillation is part of the proposed approach to preserving head-class performance, not a numerical answer to the recall question.
Is there a subtle distinction between saying the mask preserves foreground and saying the swap preserves rare-class cues?

There is. Foreground recall concerns identifying foreground regions. Preserving rare-class cues concerns retaining the information that supports recognition of rare classes through the swap. The first is relevant to the second, but a single recall figure does not establish it.
Would perfect foreground recall settle the whole question?

It would rule out missed foreground *as measured by recall*, but it would not alone establish that background swaps preserve every relevant cue or that head-logit distillation keeps head-class accuracy within the required range. The question connects mask quality to recognition outcomes; recall is only one part of that connection.
How should we phrase the uncertainty without implying the method failed?

We can say that the required pseudo-mask foreground recall is unknown: the proposal has not specified or demonstrated a threshold at which source background swaps preserve rare-class cues while head-class logit distillation protects head classes. That leaves the question open without claiming either success or failure.
And “protects head classes” is an intended effect, not an established result?

Correct. In this question, head-logit distillation is the proposed means of protecting head classes. No achieved head-class accuracy, or evidence that distillation provides that protection at a given mask recall, is stated.
Then the key point is that foreground recall needs to be high enough for the swaps not to discard rare-class cues, but we cannot put a number on “high enough” from what we have?

Exactly. That expresses why recall matters without inventing a threshold. It also leaves open whether, at whatever recall proves sufficient for rare-class cues, head-logit distillation preserves head-class performance as intended.
Can we put a number on the foreground-mask recall question as a hypothesis, without treating it as a result?

Yes. The hypothesis is that, at ≥85% foreground-mask recall, background swaps raise reversal-set tail macro-accuracy by ≥5 percentage points versus ERM, while head-logit distillation limits head-class loss to ≤1 percentage point. Neither the recall threshold nor either accuracy outcome is established by stating the hypothesis.
What does the 85% refer to exactly?

It refers to foreground-mask recall: the share of actual foreground identified as foreground by the pseudo-mask. The hypothesis concerns masks with recall of at least 85%, including exactly 85%. It is not saying that 85% of images or classes must meet an accuracy target.
Is ≥85% being proposed as the minimum recall that could possibly work?
No. It is a proposed condition under which the accuracy outcomes are hypothesized to hold. It does not establish that lower recall cannot work, or that 85% is the lowest sufficient value.
What is the precise tail-side prediction?

For the reversal set, the prediction is that swaps raise tail macro-accuracy by at least 5 percentage points compared with ERM. “At least” includes a gain of exactly 5 points; a smaller gain would not meet this part of the hypothesis.
And what is predicted for the head classes?

The prediction is that distillation limits head-class loss to at most 1 percentage point. That is a limit on a drop, not a claim that head-class performance must drop by exactly 1 point. The hypothesis does not report an observed head-class outcome.
Do both predictions have to hold at the proposed recall level?

Yes. The hypothesis combines them: at ≥85% foreground-mask recall, swaps are expected to deliver the ≥5-point reversal-set tail macro-accuracy gain versus ERM, while distillation is expected to hold head loss to ≤1 point. Meeting only one prediction would not establish the combined hypothesis.
Is the 5-point gain attributed to the swaps, and the head-loss limit to distillation?

That is how the hypothesis assigns their intended roles. It predicts a tail gain from background swaps and limited head loss with distillation. Those are proposed effects, not demonstrated causal findings.
Does reaching 85% foreground-mask recall itself show that rare-class cues survived the swaps?

No. Recall measures how much foreground the mask identifies; it does not specify which foreground information is retained or prove that the resulting swaps preserve cues useful for tail-class recognition. The accuracy prediction is a separate part of the hypothesis.
Could we say that the recall threshold guarantees the two accuracy outcomes?
Not as an established guarantee. The careful phrasing is that the hypothesis predicts those outcomes at ≥85% foreground-mask recall. Whether that prediction holds is still open.
How does “reversal-set” qualify the tail prediction?

It locates the predicted tail macro-accuracy gain in the setting where predictive background correlations reverse. The ≥5-point comparison is not stated as a gain on every possible evaluation setting.
Does this change the no-target-domain-labels condition from the original goal?
No. The hypothesis addresses the proposed background-swap and distillation approach within the goal of working without target-domain labels. It does not introduce labeled target-domain data.
Should I treat “tail” and “head” as precisely defined class lists here?

No class lists are specified in this hypothesis. It refers to tail macro-accuracy and head loss; the broader goal separately states bottom-quintile and top-quintile class macro-accuracy requirements. The hypothesis does not supply a more detailed definition of the tail or head groups.
If the tail gain reached 5 points but head loss exceeded 1 point, would that support the whole prediction?
No. It would satisfy the stated tail-side threshold but not the head-loss limit. The hypothesis requires both at the proposed recall condition.
And if results were good below 85% recall, would that alone contradict this hypothesis?

Not necessarily. The hypothesis predicts outcomes at ≥85% recall; it does not predict failure below 85%. A successful outcome below that threshold would bear on whether 85% is necessary, but necessity is not claimed here.
Can you leave me with the exact claim, clearly marked as untested?

The untested hypothesis is: at ≥85% foreground-mask recall, background swaps raise reversal-set tail macro-accuracy by ≥5 percentage points versus ERM, and head-logit distillation limits head-class loss to ≤1 percentage point.
How would we investigate the foreground-mask recall question?

The plan is to audit 200 source masks, sweep pseudo-mask thresholds around 85% foreground recall along with distillation strength, and compare BackgroundFlip-LT quintile macro-accuracy with ERM. These are planned steps, not completed measurements.
What is the purpose of auditing 200 source masks?

The audit is meant to examine the source masks in relation to the foreground-recall question before interpreting the sweep. The plan specifies 200 source masks; it does not specify an audit procedure or report any recall measurements.
Does that mean 200 target-domain masks?
No. They are explicitly source masks. The plan does not call for auditing target-domain masks or using target-domain labels.
When you say “sweep pseudo-mask thresholds around 85% recall,” is the threshold itself set to 85%?

Not necessarily. A pseudo-mask threshold is a setting that may affect which regions the mask identifies as foreground; foreground recall is the resulting measure of how much actual foreground it captures. The plan is to explore threshold settings in relation to recall around 85%, not to equate a threshold value with 85% recall.
Does the plan specify exact threshold values or a range of recall values?
No. It specifies a sweep around 85% recall, but not the individual threshold settings, the spacing between them, or precise recall endpoints.
Why focus the sweep around 85%?

The proposed hypothesis places its predicted outcomes at ≥85% foreground-mask recall. Sweeping around that point is a way to investigate the question of how mask recall relates to performance, without assuming that 85% has already been shown sufficient or necessary.
Is distillation strength swept separately from the pseudo-mask threshold?
The plan says to sweep both pseudo-mask thresholds and distillation strength. It does not specify how settings for the two will be combined, how many strengths will be tried, or any particular value.
Why vary distillation strength at all if the question is about mask recall?

The question has two linked parts: whether background swaps preserve rare-class cues and whether head-logit distillation protects head classes. Varying distillation strength lets the planned comparison consider the head-class side alongside the mask-recall side. It does not presume that any strength will meet the head-class target.
What exactly gets compared with ERM?

The planned comparison is BackgroundFlip-LT quintile macro-accuracy against ERM. In terms of the stated goal, the key comparisons are bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy and top-quintile class macro-accuracy, with the same training data used for the ERM baseline comparison.
What does the plan tell us about BackgroundFlip-LT?
It names BackgroundFlip-LT as the setting for the quintile macro-accuracy comparison. The plan does not provide further details about its construction, class counts, or evaluation procedure.
Which result would address the rare-class requirement?

The relevant result would be bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy under background reversals that is at least 5 percentage points higher than ERM’s, using identical training data. The plan proposes comparing performance; it does not say that this result has occurred.
And what would we look at for the common classes?

Top-quintile class macro-accuracy should remain within 1 percentage point of the ERM baseline, again with identical training data. The distillation-strength sweep is relevant to that constraint, but the plan reports no outcome for it.
Would a mask audit alone tell us whether the 5-point gain is achieved?

No. Auditing source masks speaks to mask quality, including the foreground-recall question. The gain is an accuracy comparison with ERM on BackgroundFlip-LT, so it cannot be read from the mask audit alone.
Likewise, would reaching 85% recall establish that head-class loss stays within 1 point?

No. Foreground recall is a mask measure, while the head-class condition is an accuracy comparison. The plan includes a distillation-strength sweep and a quintile macro-accuracy comparison precisely because recall alone does not establish both outcomes.
Does the plan already identify the best threshold or distillation strength?
No. It proposes sweeping those settings; it neither selects a best setting nor reports results from any setting.
Can the comparison tell us whether the proposed ≥85% recall hypothesis holds?

It is intended to inform that question by relating the mask-recall region being explored to tail and head quintile macro-accuracy versus ERM. Whether it supports the predicted ≥5-point tail gain and ≤1-point head loss depends on results that are not supplied here.
Does the plan claim that recall below 85% will fail?
No. Sweeping around 85% does not assert failure below it. The plan investigates performance near the proposed threshold rather than declaring a necessary cutoff.
Are we committing to a particular way of measuring foreground recall in the audit?

The plan specifies an audit of 200 source masks and a sweep around 85% recall, but it does not state the audit protocol or the measurement procedure. Those details should not be treated as already decided.
What is the cleanest way to describe the whole plan without making it sound completed?

We plan to audit 200 source masks, sweep pseudo-mask thresholds around 85% foreground recall and vary distillation strength, then compare BackgroundFlip-LT quintile macro-accuracy with ERM. The comparisons are intended to assess the rare-class gain and head-class preservation goals; no audit or accuracy result is yet stated.
Can we make the mask-recall investigation more concrete as an activity?

Audit 200 source masks, train background-swap variants at 80%, 85%, and 90% foreground-mask recall with two distillation weights, and score quintile macro-accuracy on BackgroundFlip-LT. This specifies the activity, not its results.
Are 80%, 85%, and 90% pseudo-mask threshold values?

No. They are foreground-mask recall levels for the swap variants. A pseudo-mask threshold is a setting that affects the mask; recall describes how much actual foreground the resulting mask captures. The activity does not state the threshold values used to obtain those recall levels.
What is being audited, and how many?
The activity calls for an audit of 200 source masks. It does not specify an audit protocol or report what the audit finds.
Does “source masks” imply access to target-domain labels?
No. The masks named here are source masks, and the activity does not introduce target-domain labels. That is consistent with the goal of working without them.
Why train variants at all three recall levels rather than only 85%?

The three levels let the activity examine performance below, at, and above the proposed 85% recall point. Including 80% and 90% does not, by itself, establish that 85% is a necessary or sufficient cutoff.
Are the distillation weights also specified numerically?
No. The activity specifies two distillation weights, but gives neither their values nor a rule for choosing them. It also does not report which weight, if either, better protects head-class accuracy.
What does changing a distillation weight mean at this level of description?

It means varying the strength assigned to head-logit distillation in the proposed training approach. The activity names that variation without specifying an objective function or implementation details.
Is the activity replacing head-logit distillation with the background swaps?
No. It trains swap variants at the specified recall levels and uses two distillation weights. The swaps and distillation remain distinct parts of the approach being examined.
What will be scored after training?

BackgroundFlip-LT quintile macro-accuracy will be scored. That keeps the performance assessment focused on class groups rather than only an aggregate accuracy figure. No scores are supplied in the activity.
How does that score relate to the rare-class and head-class goals?

Bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy is the relevant measure for the rare-class gain, and top-quintile class macro-accuracy is the relevant measure for head-class preservation. The goal calls for a 5-percentage-point bottom-quintile gain over ERM under background reversals and top-quintile performance within 1 percentage point of ERM, using identical training data. Scoring BackgroundFlip-LT quintile macro-accuracy provides the group-level performance information relevant to those comparisons; this activity states no outcome.
Does the activity itself say an ERM score was obtained?

No. It specifies auditing, training the recall-level variants at two distillation weights, and scoring their BackgroundFlip-LT quintile macro-accuracy. ERM remains the comparison baseline in the goal, but no ERM score is reported here.
Could we infer that the 90%-recall variant will have the best tail accuracy?

No. Higher foreground-mask recall means fewer foreground omissions by that measure, but the activity gives no accuracy results or ordering of the three variants. It does not say which recall level performs best.
Could we infer that one of the two distillation weights keeps head loss within 1 point?
No. Using two weights creates settings to examine; it does not establish the head-class outcome for either one.
Is the 200-mask audit a performance score for BackgroundFlip-LT?
No. The audit concerns source masks, while the BackgroundFlip-LT score concerns quintile macro-accuracy after training the variants. Those are different parts of the activity.
Does the activity specify which classes appear in each quintile?
No class membership lists are provided. The activity specifies quintile macro-accuracy as the score, without further defining the groups.
What can we say about how many training settings this involves?
We can say there are three specified recall levels—80%, 85%, and 90%—and two distillation weights. The activity does not spell out additional training settings or implementation details.
What is the careful one-sentence description of the activity?

Audit 200 source masks, train 80%-, 85%-, and 90%-foreground-recall background-swap variants at two distillation weights, and score BackgroundFlip-LT quintile macro-accuracy, without presuming any audit or accuracy result.
What were the BackgroundFlip-LT scores for the 85%-recall swaps with distillation?
Tail macro-accuracy was 34%, compared with 28% for ERM. Head macro-accuracy was 71.5%, compared with 72% for ERM.
How large are those differences in percentage points?
The tail score is 6 percentage points higher than ERM’s: 34% minus 28%. The head score is 0.5 percentage points lower: 71.5% versus 72%.
Does “85%-recall” mean the tail accuracy was 85%?
No. The 85% refers to foreground-mask recall for this swap variant. Its measured tail macro-accuracy on BackgroundFlip-LT was 34%.
Can I describe the tail difference as a 6% improvement?
“6 percentage points higher” is more precise. The figures are 34% and 28%, whose difference is 6 percentage points; calling it a 6% improvement could be mistaken for a relative percentage change.
And the head result—is it accurate to say the method matched ERM exactly?
No. The reported head score is 71.5%, while ERM’s is 72%. They are close, but the swap-with-distillation score is 0.5 percentage points lower.
Does this tell us how the 80%- and 90%-recall variants scored?
No. These figures are for the 85%-recall swaps with distillation. No scores for the 80%- or 90%-recall variants are stated here, so the three variants cannot be ranked from this evidence.
Do we know which of the two distillation weights produced these numbers?
The reported result identifies swaps with distillation at 85% recall, but it does not identify a distillation weight. It would be inaccurate to attach these scores to a particular weight.
Can we attribute the 6-point tail difference specifically to the background swaps?
The reported comparison is between the 85%-recall swap-with-distillation setting and ERM. It gives their score difference, but does not isolate the effect of swaps from the effect of distillation.
Likewise, do the head scores prove distillation caused the small head difference?
No. The scores show a 0.5-percentage-point head difference between the reported setting and ERM. Without a result isolating distillation, these figures alone do not establish its separate effect.
What does macro-accuracy tell me about the tail figure?

It is a class-group measure, rather than a single overall accuracy across all images. The stated tail macro-accuracy is 34% for the 85%-recall swap-with-distillation setting and 28% for ERM on BackgroundFlip-LT. The evidence does not provide individual class scores.
Should I read the head and tail comparisons as coming from the same reported setting?
Yes. Both reported scores describe the 85%-recall swaps with distillation on BackgroundFlip-LT, each compared with the corresponding ERM score: 34% versus 28% for tail, and 71.5% versus 72% for head.
Does the 85% figure tell us anything about what the 200-mask audit found?
It identifies the foreground-mask recall of the reported swap variant. The evidence does not give findings from the audit of 200 source masks, so it does not tell us what that audit found.
Could these numbers establish that 85% recall is the minimum needed?
No. They report performance at 85% recall, not a minimum sufficient recall. In particular, without the other recall variants’ scores, these figures cannot determine what happens below or above 85%.
What can we say about uncertainty or consistency across runs?

No uncertainty estimates, run-to-run variation, or number of runs are given with these scores. The stated evidence is the reported BackgroundFlip-LT comparison, not a measurement of how consistent that comparison is.
Give me a careful statement of the result that does not overattribute it.

On BackgroundFlip-LT, the 85%-foreground-recall swaps with distillation yielded 34% tail macro-accuracy versus ERM’s 28%, a 6-percentage-point difference. Head macro-accuracy was 71.5% versus ERM’s 72%, a 0.5-percentage-point difference in ERM’s favor. These figures describe the combined setting; they do not isolate the effects of swaps or distillation.
Which setting should we select?

Select the 85%-foreground-recall background swaps with head-logit distillation. The stated reason is their BackgroundFlip-LT result versus ERM: a 6-percentage-point tail macro-accuracy gain and a 0.5-percentage-point head macro-accuracy loss.
Is the 85% figure an accuracy score?
No. It is foreground-mask recall for the selected swap setting. The 6-point gain and 0.5-point loss describe its tail and head macro-accuracy differences relative to ERM on BackgroundFlip-LT.
Why select a setting that has a head loss?
The decision weighs the reported 6-point tail gain alongside a comparatively small, 0.5-point head loss versus ERM. It does not describe the head result as an improvement or as exactly equal to ERM.
Does the decision select swaps by themselves, or the combined approach?
The combined approach: 85%-recall swaps **with head-logit distillation**. The decision does not select swaps without distillation.
Can we say head-logit distillation alone caused the 0.5-point loss to be small?
No. The decision selects the combined setting based on its reported comparison with ERM. That comparison does not, on its own, isolate distillation’s separate effect.
Does choosing 85% mean it is the minimum foreground recall required?
No. The decision identifies a setting to use; it does not establish a minimum recall threshold or make a claim about every setting above or below 85%.
Are we declaring it the best-performing recall setting?
The decision does not make that ranking. Its stated basis is the BackgroundFlip-LT gain and loss for the selected 85%-recall setting versus ERM, not a claim that it outperforms every other setting.
What should stay attached to the numbers when I describe the decision?

Keep the setting, evaluation context, and baseline attached: **85%-recall swaps with head-logit distillation**, evaluated on **BackgroundFlip-LT**, with a **6-percentage-point tail gain** and a **0.5-percentage-point head loss** versus **ERM**. Without that context, the numbers could sound like general performance guarantees.
